content: The global food system, while imposing significant environmental costs, provides employment to over a billion people. To achieve diets that are both healthy and sustainable, it is essential to consider the full spectrum of environmental and social consequences associated with the global food system. This must be done in a way that supports local livelihoods and promotes equity. Currently, 6.1 billion people face some form of nutritional challenge, including undernourishment, overweight adults, and overweight children under five years of age. Agriculture employs over one billion people globally, but it is also responsible for 80% of global deforestation, 29% of greenhouse gas emissions, and 70% of freshwater use. Addressing these issues requires a careful assessment of environmental, social, and economic determinants to mainstream biodiversity for nutrition and health. Governments play a critical role in shaping and regulating food systems to create environments that enable access to sustainable, healthy diets. This requires coordinated action across multiple sectors and the involvement of various stakeholders, including governments at all levels, civil society, and the private sector. Integrated analyses of sociocultural and economic conditions influencing malnutrition and disease outcomes must be informed by robust, disaggregated data that accounts for gender and socioeconomic status. Dietary shifts have not been uniform across population groups, with vulnerable populations experiencing disproportionate impacts. Disaggregated data is crucial to understanding access to healthy foods and the health outcomes of dietary changes. Such data can help identify the drivers of change in the food system and pinpoint areas where action is most needed. Vulnerability and adaptation assessments tailored to specific population contexts are essential tools. These assessments should consider factors such as land use, climate change, and agrobiodiversity loss. Establishing relevant baselines, developing projections to assess the future impacts of biodiversity loss and climate change on malnutrition, and identifying appropriate responses to mitigate and monitor related risks over time are critical steps. Integrated approaches, such as One Health and Ecohealth, facilitate cross-sectoral coordination and policy coherence in managing both land-based and aquatic agroecosystems. These approaches have been increasingly recognized in international policy developments for their value in managing agroecosystems and improving related health outcomes. Agroecology, which emphasizes participatory processes, knowledge co-production, and equity, offers a promising example of ecosystem-based approaches to sustainable food production. Agroecological approaches prioritize natural processes, minimize the use of external inputs, and promote local knowledge and participatory practices. They also address social inequalities and recognize the interconnected nature of agrifood systems, from production to consumption. The transformation toward a sustainable and resilient food system capable of delivering safe, healthy, nutritious, and affordable foods requires alignment among various actors, policies, and sectors. This transformation demands integrated indicators and ongoing monitoring of progress and outcomes. Biodiversity's central relevance to achieving healthy, sustainable diets is not yet fully reflected in global indicators, such as those for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2. Ending malnutrition in all its forms, while supporting sustainable development, requires linking efforts across sectors and SDGs, including those aimed at ending poverty (SDG 1), hunger (SDG 2), and promoting responsible consumption and production (SDG 12). This effort must also consider co-benefits and trade-offs for SDG 3 (health), SDG 13 (climate action), SDG 14 (life below water), and SDG 15 (life on land). Intergovernmental organizations have begun enhancing efforts to link food biodiversity to human nutrition and healthy diets. Initiatives such as the Biodiversity for Food and Nutrition (BFN) project provide examples of how to operationalize biodiversity mainstreaming through research, capacity development, and best practices. Six core building blocks for mainstreaming biodiversity in nutrition and health have been identified: knowledge development and co-production, enabling environments, integration into research and policy, conservation and wider use of biodiversity, education and awareness-raising, and monitoring and evaluation. These building blocks provide a framework for aligning and monitoring progress against international commitments to eradicate hunger and malnutrition.
